question: Can a state licensing board deny me an occupational license because of a criminal conviction, and how can I challenge the denial?

groups: duties and responsibilities of the occupation
Department of Licensing and Consumer Protection

gold_sections.why: Non-health occupations: a board may act against (and direct the Mayor to deny) an applicant convicted of an offense directly related to the occupation; it may not consider unrelated convictions, may not ask until the applicant is otherwise qualified, may not consider sealed, expunged, vacated or pardoned convictions, juvenile adjudications or non-conviction information; the totality-of-factors test (clear and convincing evidence, rehabilitation and fitness, the District's interest in employing people with records).

Licensing criteria (no directly related conviction, as determined under 47-2853.17(c-1)(2)); application to the Mayor; the right to petition a board at any time for an early determination of disqualification, decided within 90 days.

Challenge procedure: opportunity for a hearing before denial (with exceptions), the written notice required before a conviction-based hearing, 45 business days to respond and 45 business days for the board's final decision, certified-mail hearing notice 15 days ahead with information on legal resources, counsel, subpoenas the board must issue at the person's reasonable request, 90-day written decision after a hearing, panel decisions and rehearing before the full board (no appeal until the full board rules).
Any person aggrieved by a board's final decision may appeal to the D.C. Court of Appeals under 2-510.

Health occupations (separate law): a board may deny a license for a conviction of an offense related to the occupation, and must consider the listed factors (relation to duties, nature and seriousness, time elapsed, age, rehabilitation, work history, references).

Health occupation boards must offer a hearing before denying a license (same exceptions pattern), with certified-mail notice, counsel and a 90-day written decision; a board may delegate hearings and final decisions to a panel of 3 or more members or an administrative law judge under the Mayor's rules (i).
Appeal of a health board's final decision to the D.C. Court of Appeals under 2-510.
Health occupation applicants must establish they have not been convicted of an offense related to the occupation.

Judicial review: written petition for review in the D.C. Court of Appeals, filed within the time the court sets by rule; the court may affirm, modify or set aside; grounds such as arbitrary or capricious action or lack of substantial evidence; filing does not automatically stay the decision.

Which non-health occupations the subchapter covers and which are regulated elsewhere (c), among others: attorneys by the Court of Appeals; taxicab and limousine operators by the Department of For-Hire Vehicles; commercial drivers and commercial bicycle operators by the Department of Public Works; special police, security alarm agents and private correctional officers by the Metropolitan Police Department; insurance and securities; boxers and wrestlers.

Board powers: decide qualification questions the Mayor refers, binding on the Mayor (3); hear and decide protests from a person denied a license by a Mayor's licensing official for not meeting the board's eligibility standards, binding on the Mayor (5).

The Mayor issues licenses to those who meet board standards, refers any question about an applicant's qualification to the board, and then takes the action the board determines (a)(1); the Mayor arranges hearings when a board asks (a)(4).

Contested-case rules the board hearing follows (47-2853.22 c, 3-1205.19 c): notice of the issues, burden of proof on the proponent of an order, the right to present evidence, rebut and cross-examine, an exclusive record, and a written adverse decision with findings of fact and conclusions of law.

Office of Administrative Hearings: its chapter covers Department of Health (a)(1) and Department of Licensing and Consumer Protection (b)(2A) adjudications, but a board keeps its own authority to hear cases (h); a licensing board may delegate a denial hearing and order to OAH, and the OAH order is appealable to the board (i)(1).

OAH orders take effect when issued; a motion for reconsideration or a new trial is due within 10 calendar days of service (a); the delegating board hears any appeal from the ALJ's order (b); contested-case orders are reviewed in the D.C. Court of Appeals under the 2-510 standards (e), (g).

answer:
Yes, within limits. Under D.C.'s general licensing law, a board may deny a license only for a conviction directly related to the occupation [N1], never for an unrelated one [N2]. It cannot ask about your record until you are otherwise qualified [N3], or consider sealed, expunged, vacated or pardoned convictions [N4], juvenile adjudications, arrests, diversion or deferred sentencing [N16]. It weighs whether the offense's elements are directly related, by clear and convincing evidence, to the job's duties [N5], rehabilitation evidence (no reoffending, time passed, work history, references) [N6], and D.C.'s interest in employing people with records [N17].

To challenge: petition anytime, even pre-training, for an early ruling [N7], due within 90 days [N8]. Before a hearing, the board must explain in writing which conviction it relies on and why, with records [N10]; you have 45 business days to respond [N11], then it has 45 business days to decide [N18]. You must be offered a hearing unless no material facts are disputed or the denial rests only on age, education, experience, exams or fees [N9]; an administrative law judge may hear it, appealable to the board [N20]. Denials need written findings [N22]. Protest a licensing official's denial to the board [N21]. Appeal final decisions to the D.C. Court of Appeals [N12] within the time its rules set [N23], after any requested full-board rehearing [N19].

Health-profession boards follow a separate law: denial for a related conviction [N13], weighing seriousness and other factors [N14], after offering a hearing [N15], appealable likewise [N12].

gaps: The early petition (47-2853.12 n) is optional and can be filed at any time; it is modeled as an alternative path from the start that ends with the board's determination, after which the person may apply.

47-2853.22 gives two decision clocks: for conviction-based actions the board has 45 business days after the applicant's response to issue its final decision (a-1.2.B), and after any hearing a written final decision within 90 days (h). The model puts the 45-business-day clock on the final decision; how the two interact when a hearing is held is not stated.

A hearing is not required where the denial rests solely on minimum age, education, experience, examination or fee requirements, or where no material facts are at issue (47-2853.22 a); the hearing path is modeled as conditional on material facts being at issue. The statute speaks of an 'opportunity' for a hearing and does not say how or when it must be requested.

If the applicant does not respond within 45 business days the model goes straight to the final decision; the statute does not state a consequence, and a board may hear and determine the matter if the person fails to appear (47-2853.22 g).

Off the main path: an optional settlement conference and consent decree (47-2853.22 b); hearings and final decisions by a panel of 3 or more members, with a right to rehearing before the full board, and no appeal to the Court of Appeals until the full board rules if rehearing is requested (47-2853.22 i); the board acts by majority of members present and voting and directs the Mayor to deny (47-2853.17 a, c).
The deadline for filing the petition for review is set by D.C. Court of Appeals rule, not by statute (2-510 a), and filing does not by itself stay the denial.

confirm_qualified models 47-2853.17(c-1)(1)(A)(i), which bars inquiry into the conviction until the board finds the applicant otherwise qualified; it is a timing prohibition, not a duty to make that finding. The qualification finding itself is presupposed (the Mayor refers qualification questions to the board under 47-2853.08(3) and 47-2853.10(a)(1)) and is modeled as the gate otherwise_qualified.

Who hears it: 47-2853.22 provides a hearing before the board or a panel of 3 or more members (i). 2-1831.03 brings Department of Health (a)(1) and DLCP (b)(2A) adjudications under the Office of Administrative Hearings, but (h) keeps a board's authority to hear cases itself, and (i)(1) lets a licensing board delegate the hearing and order on a proposed denial to OAH. The OAH order is then appealable to the board (2-1831.16 b), and a motion for reconsideration or new trial is due within 10 calendar days of service (2-1831.16 a). Health boards may delegate to a panel or an administrative law judge under the Mayor's rules (3-1205.19 i). The OAH path is not modeled.

Alternative route not modeled: a person denied by a Mayor's licensing official because they do not meet the board's eligibility standards may protest to the board, and the board's determination binds the Mayor (47-2853.08(5)).

The hearing follows 2-509 (47-2853.22 c): the proponent of an order has the burden of proof (2-509 b), but the statutes do not say whether the board or the applicant is the proponent when a license application is denied; 47-2853.17(c-1)(2)(A) separately requires the offense's elements to be directly related by clear and convincing evidence. An adverse decision must be written with findings of fact and conclusions of law (2-509 e).

The statutes do not say whether a ruling on an early petition (47-2853.12 n) is a 'final decision' that can be appealed under 47-2853.23, or whether a denial made without a hearing is a 'contested case' reviewable under 2-510(a).

Health occupations (Chapter 12 of Title 3) follow a parallel but different process: denial for a conviction 'related to' the occupation with the 3-1205.14(f) factors, hearing under 3-1205.19 and appeal under 3-1205.20, but without the 'otherwise qualified' timing rule, the sealed-record and non-conviction bars, the written conviction notice with 45 business days to respond, or the early petition. 3-1205.14(a)(3) defines 'convicted', for that paragraph, to include a nolo contendere or Alford plea and a deferred sentence or deferred judgment; (a)(4), the related-offense ground, does not define the term.

notes: D.C. has a general statute for the non-health occupations licensed through the Department of Licensing and Consumer Protection boards (Chapter 28 subchapter of Title 47, 47-2853.01 et seq.): 47-2853.12(a)(1) makes 'no directly related conviction' a licensing criterion; 47-2853.17(a)(5), (c)(1) lets a board direct the Mayor to deny on that ground; 47-2853.17(c-1) bars inquiry until the applicant is otherwise qualified, bars considering sealed, expunged, vacated, pardoned or Youth Rehabilitation Act set-aside convictions, juvenile adjudications and non-conviction information (deferred sentencing agreements, diversion, arrests without conviction), bars considering convictions not directly related, and sets the totality-of-factors test, which also includes the District's interest in promoting employment opportunities for individuals with criminal records (c-1.2.C); 47-2853.12(n) allows an early petition decided within 90 days; 47-2853.22 gives the notice, 45-business-day response, hearing, counsel, subpoena and decision rules; 47-2853.23 and 2-510 give review in the D.C. Court of Appeals. If a suspension or revocation based on a directly related conviction rests on a conviction later overturned, it ends automatically (47-2853.24 b). Health occupations under Chapter 12 of Title 3 use a looser 'related to the occupation' standard (3-1205.03 a.1, 3-1205.14 a.4) with the 3-1205.14(f) factors, a mandatory criminal background check (3-1205.22), hearing (3-1205.19) and appeal (3-1205.20); the sealed-record and timing protections of 47-2853.17(c-1) do not appear there, and the sealing law lets a licensing agency see sealed records for offenses that may disqualify a person, to the extent it could before, except records sealed under 16-806(a)(2) (citations, arrests and charges only for being a fugitive from justice) (16-801 a.5.D, 16-807 d.1.C); a person whose record is sealed commits no perjury or false statement by not disclosing it in response to any inquiry (16-807 b). Many occupations are regulated outside these two subchapters by their own statutes and agencies (47-2853.04 c: attorneys; notaries; public-school and UDC teachers and principals; insurance agents and brokers, securities agents and brokers, and investment advisers; hackers and taxicab and limousine operators; commercial drivers and commercial bicycle operators; special police, security alarm agents and private correctional officers; boxers, wrestlers and contest officials; clinical laboratory directors and technicians; veterinarians; funeral directors), and those may have different conviction rules. Security officers ((a)(40)) are not on the (c) exception list. 47-2853.17(a)(5) as downloaded ends with a stray quotation mark (codification artifact); the substance is unaffected.
